name: Cybersecurity Act
evidence_rating: thin: one Commission evaluation based on interviews and surveys (no outcome indicators); no independent impact studies
summary: The Cybersecurity Act made the EU cyber agency ENISA permanent and created an EU-wide certification system for ICT products. The Commission's 2026 evaluation found ENISA delivered nearly all its planned work but lacked resources and indicators, while certification badly underperformed: the first scheme took almost five years and the cloud scheme stalled. The Commission has proposed replacing the Act; no independent study measures its effect on cyber resilience.

indicators.objective: Increase capabilities and preparedness of Member States and businesses; improve cooperation; raise awareness; strengthen trust through certification of ICT products and services

indicators.indicator: Trainings, good practices, threat landscape reports, exercises (e.g. Cyber Europe), support requests handled
indicators.evidence: Evaluation: ENISA delivered nearly all planned outputs and stakeholders value its work, but 'with no sufficient indicators in place' the assessment relies mainly on interviews and surveys; insufficient resources and hiring problems caused delays.

indicators.indicator: Number of certification schemes adopted under the framework
indicators.evidence: One scheme (EUCC, common criteria) adopted in early 2024, 57 months after initiation; cloud scheme (EUCS) stalled over data-sovereignty disputes; 5G scheme not adopted. Framework judged unable to reduce fragmentation.

indicators.indicator: Reduced cost of obtaining an ICT security certificate
Increase in cyber awareness among EU citizens (e.g. awareness quiz scores)
indicators.evidence: No time series reported in the evaluation.

indicators.indicator: Help reduce the cost of cyber incidents, estimated at 0.41% of EU GDP (about EUR 55bn)

literature.citation: European Commission (2017), Impact Assessment accompanying the Cybersecurity Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2017) 501), SWD(2017) 500
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the Cybersecurity Act proposal (executive summary SWD(2017) 501)
literature.headline: Preferred option: permanent, reinforced ENISA plus an EU ICT security certification framework enabling mutual recognition; moderate extra EU budget cost; benefits not quantified (context: cyber incidents cost about 0.41% of EU GDP)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected a stronger EU cyber agency and EU-wide certification to reduce fragmentation and raise trust, without quantifying the benefits.

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), Report on the evaluation of ENISA and the European Cybersecurity Certification Framework, COM(2026) 9 (SWD(2026) 2)
literature.title: Report on the evaluation of ENISA and the European Cybersecurity Certification Framework
literature.method: evaluation (interviews, surveys, document review; external study completed Dec 2024)
literature.headline: ENISA delivered nearly all planned outputs but lacked indicators and resources; the certification framework failed to reduce fragmentation: first scheme (EUCC) took 57 months and was adopted only in early 2024, cloud scheme stalled over data-sovereignty debates
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's evaluation found the EU cyber agency does useful work but is stretched, while the certification system has been slow and has not reduced fragmentation: only one scheme was adopted in five years.

literature.citation: European Commission (2026), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Cybersecurity Act 2 (executive summary SWD(2026) 12), SWD(2026) 11
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Cybersecurity Act 2 (executive summary SWD(2026) 12)
literature.headline: Proposes repealing and replacing Regulation 2019/881: reformed certification framework with scheme maintenance; ENISA costs up to EUR 161.3m over five years; compliance savings for businesses of up to EUR 14.6bn
literature.summary_plain: Building on the evaluation, the Commission proposed in 2026 to replace the Cybersecurity Act and fix its certification process.
